Quasar
A quasar is an extremely <color=#3366CC>luminous</color> <color=#3366CC>active galactic nucleus</color> (AGN). It is sometimes known as a quasi-stellar object,
abbreviated QSO. The emission from an AGN is powered by <color=#3366CC>accretion</color> onto a <color=#3366CC>supermassive black hole</color> with a mass
ranging from millions to tens of billions of <color=#3366CC>solar masses</color>, surrounded by a gaseous <color=#3366CC>accretion disc</color>. Gas in the disc falling
towards the black hole heats up and releases <color=#3366CC>energy</color> in the form of <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic radiation</color>. The radiant energy of
quasars is enormous; the most powerful quasars have <color=#3366CC>luminosities</color> thousands of times greater than that of a <color=#3366CC>galaxy</color>
such as the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color>. Quasars are usually categorized as a subclass of the more general category of AGN. The
<color=#3366CC>redshifts</color> of quasars are of <color=#3366CC>cosmological origin</color>.
The term quasar originated as a <color=#3366CC>contraction</color> of "quasi-stellar [star-like] radio source"—because they were first identified
during the 1950s as sources of radio-wave emission of unknown physical origin—and when identified in photographic
images at visible wavelengths, they resembled faint, star-like points of light. High-resolution images of quasars,
particularly from the <color=#3366CC>Hubble Space Telescope</color>, have shown that quasars occur in the centers of galaxies, and that
some host galaxies are strongly <color=#3366CC>interacting</color> or <color=#3366CC>merging</color> galaxies. As with other categories of AGN, the observed
properties of a quasar depend on many factors, including the mass of the black hole, the rate of gas accretion, the
orientation of the accretion disc relative to the observer, the presence or absence of a <color=#3366CC>jet</color>, and the degree of
<color=#3366CC>obscuration</color> by gas and <color=#3366CC>dust</color> within the host galaxy.
About a million quasars have been identified with reliable <color=#3366CC>spectroscopic</color> redshifts, and between 2-3 million identified in
photometric catalogs. The nearest known quasar is about 600 million <color=#3366CC>light-years</color> from Earth, while the record for the
most distant known AGN is at a redshift of 10.1, corresponding to a <color=#3366CC>comoving distance</color> of 31.6 billion light-years, or a
look-back time of 13.2 billion years.
Quasar discovery surveys have shown that quasar activity was more common in the distant past; the peak epoch was
approximately 10 billion years ago. Concentrations of multiple quasars are known as <color=#3366CC>large quasar groups</color> and may
constitute some of the <color=#3366CC>largest known structures</color> in the universe if the observed groups are good tracers of mass
distribution.
Naming
The term quasar was first used in an article by <color=#3366CC>astrophysicist</color> Hong-Yee Chiu in May 1964, in Physics Today, to
describe certain astronomically puzzling objects:
So far, the clumsily long name "quasi-stellar radio sources" is used to describe these objects. Because the nature of
these objects is entirely unknown, it is hard to prepare a short, appropriate nomenclature for them so that their essential
properties are obvious from their name. For convenience, the abbreviated form "quasar" will be used throughout this
paper.
History of observation and interpretation
Background
Between 1917 and 1922, it became clear from work by Heber Doust Curtis, Ernst Öpik, and others that some objects
("<color=#3366CC>nebulae</color>") seen by astronomers were in fact distant <color=#3366CC>galaxies</color> like the Milky Way. But when <color=#3366CC>radio astronomy</color> began in
the 1950s, astronomers detected, among the galaxies, a small number of anomalous objects with properties that defied
explanation.
The objects emitted large amounts of radiation of many frequencies, but no source could be located optically, or in
some cases, only a faint and <color=#3366CC>point-like</color> object somewhat like a distant <color=#3366CC>star</color>. The <color=#3366CC>spectral lines</color> of these objects, which
identify the <color=#3366CC>chemical elements</color> of which the object is composed, were also extremely strange and defied explanation.
Some of them changed their <color=#3366CC>luminosity</color> very rapidly in the optical range and even more rapidly in the X-ray range,
suggesting an upper limit on their size, perhaps no larger than the <color=#3366CC>Solar System</color>. This implies an extremely high power
density. Considerable discussion took place over what these objects might be. They were described as "quasi-stellar
[meaning: star-like] radio sources", or "quasi-stellar objects" (QSOs), a name which reflected their unknown nature, and
this became shortened to "quasar".
Early observations (1960s and earlier)
The first quasars (3C 48 and <color=#3366CC>3C 273</color>) were discovered in the late 1950s, as radio sources in all-sky radio surveys. They
were first noted as radio sources with no corresponding visible object. Using small telescopes and the Lovell Telescope
as an <color=#3366CC>interferometer</color>, they were shown to have a very small angular size. By 1960, hundreds of these objects had been
recorded and published in the Third Cambridge Catalogue while astronomers scanned the skies for their optical
counterparts. In 1963, a definite identification of the radio source 3C 48 with an optical object was published by <color=#3366CC>Allan</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sandage</color> and Thomas A. Matthews. Astronomers had detected what appeared to be a faint blue star at the location of
the radio source and obtained its spectrum, which contained many unknown broad emission lines. The anomalous
spectrum defied interpretation.
British-Australian astronomer John Bolton made many early observations of quasars, including a breakthrough in 1962.
Another radio source, <color=#3366CC>3C 273</color>, was predicted to undergo five <color=#3366CC>occultations</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Moon</color>. Measurements taken by Cyril
Hazard and John Bolton during one of the occultations using the Parkes Radio Telescope allowed Maarten Schmidt to
find a visible counterpart to the radio source and obtain an <color=#3366CC>optical spectrum</color> using the 200 in Hale Telescope on Mount
Palomar. This spectrum revealed the same strange emission lines. Schmidt was able to demonstrate that these were
likely to be the ordinary <color=#3366CC>spectral lines</color> of hydrogen redshifted by 15.8%—at the time, a high redshift, since only a
handful of much fainter galaxies were known to have a higher redshift. If this was due to the physical motion of the
"star", then 3C 273 was receding at an enormous velocity, around 47,000 km/s, far beyond the speed of any known star
and defying any obvious explanation. Nor would an extreme velocity help to explain 3C 273's huge radio emissions. If
the redshift was cosmological (now known to be correct), the large distance implied that 3C 273 was far more luminous
than any galaxy, but much more compact. Also, 3C 273 was bright enough to detect on archival photographs dating
back to the 1900s; it was found to be variable on yearly timescales, implying that a substantial fraction of the light was
emitted from a region less than 1 light-year in size, tiny compared to a galaxy.
Although it raised many questions, Schmidt's discovery quickly revolutionized quasar observation. Schmidt, Greenstein,
and Oke quickly identified the strange spectrum of 3C 48 as <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color> and <color=#3366CC>magnesium</color> redshifted by 37%. Shortly
afterwards, two more quasar spectra in 1964 and five more in 1965 were also confirmed as ordinary light that had been
redshifted to an extreme degree.
Development of physical understanding (1960s)
An extreme redshift could imply a great distance and velocity, but could also be due to extreme mass or an unknown
law of nature. Extreme velocity and distance would also imply immense power output, which lacked explanation. The
small sizes were confirmed by <color=#3366CC>interferometry</color> and by observing how quickly the quasar as a whole varied in output, and
by their inability to be seen with even the most powerful visible-light telescopes as anything more than faint, starlike
points of light. However, if they were small and far away, their power output would have to be immense for their size,
making them difficult to explain. Equally, if they were very small and much closer to this galaxy, it would be easy to
explain their apparent power output, but less easy to explain their redshifts and lack of detectable movement against
the background of the universe.
Schmidt noted that redshift is also associated with the expansion of the universe, as codified in <color=#3366CC>Hubble's law</color>. If the
measured redshift was due to relative velocity caused by inflation, then this would support an interpretation of very
distant objects with extraordinarily high <color=#3366CC>luminosity</color> and power output, far beyond any object observed to date. This
extreme luminosity would also explain the large radio signal. Schmidt concluded that 3C 273 could either be an
individual star around 10 km wide within (or near to) this galaxy, or a distant active galactic nucleus. Schmidt stated that
for quasars to be distant and extremely powerful objects seemed more likely to be correct.
Schmidt's explanation for the high redshift was not widely accepted at the time. A major concern was the enormous
amount of energy these objects would have to be radiating if they were distant. In the 1960s, no commonly accepted
mechanism could account for this. The currently accepted explanation, that it is due to <color=#3366CC>matter</color> in an <color=#3366CC>accretion disc</color>
falling into a <color=#3366CC>supermassive black hole</color>, was only suggested in 1964 by <color=#3366CC>Edwin E. Salpeter</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yakov Zeldovich</color>, and
even then it was rejected by many astronomers, as at this time the existence of <color=#3366CC>black holes</color> at all was widely seen as
theoretical.
Various explanations were proposed during the 1960s and 1970s, each with its own problems. It was suggested that
quasars were nearby objects, and that their redshift was not due to the <color=#3366CC>expansion of space</color> but rather to light escaping
a deep gravitational well. This would require a massive object, which would also explain the high luminosities.
However, a star of sufficient mass to produce the measured redshift would be unstable and in excess of the Hayashi
limit. Quasars also show <color=#3366CC>forbidden</color> spectral emission lines, previously only seen in hot gaseous nebulae of low density,
which would be too diffuse to both generate the observed power and fit within a deep gravitational well. There were
also serious concerns regarding the idea of cosmologically distant quasars. One strong argument against them was
that they implied energies that were far in excess of known energy conversion processes, including <color=#3366CC>nuclear fusion</color>.
There were suggestions that quasars were made of some hitherto unknown stable form of <color=#3366CC>antimatter</color> in similarly
unknown types of region of space, and that this might account for their brightness. Others speculated that quasars
were a <color=#3366CC>white hole</color> end of a <color=#3366CC>wormhole</color>, or a <color=#3366CC>chain reaction</color> of numerous <color=#3366CC>supernovae</color>.
Eventually, starting from about the 1970s, many lines of evidence (including the first <color=#3366CC>X-ray</color> <color=#3366CC>space observatories</color>,
knowledge of <color=#3366CC>black holes</color> and modern models of <color=#3366CC>cosmology</color>) gradually demonstrated that the quasar redshifts are
genuine and due to the <color=#3366CC>expansion of space</color>, that quasars are in fact as powerful and as distant as Schmidt and some
other astronomers had suggested, and that their energy source is matter from an accretion disc falling onto a
supermassive black hole. This included crucial evidence from optical and X-ray viewing of quasar host galaxies, finding
of "intervening" absorption lines, which explained various spectral anomalies, observations from <color=#3366CC>gravitational lensing</color>,
Gunn's 1971 finding that galaxies containing quasars showed the same redshift as the quasars, and Kristian's 1973
finding that the "fuzzy" surrounding of many quasars was consistent with a less luminous host galaxy.
This model also fits well with other observations suggesting that many galaxies have a massive central black hole. It
would also explain why quasars are more common in the early universe: as a quasar draws matter from its accretion
disc, there comes a point when there is less matter nearby, and energy production falls off or ceases, as the quasar
becomes a more ordinary type of galaxy.
The accretion-disc energy-production mechanism was finally modeled in the 1970s, and black holes were also directly
detected (including evidence showing that supermassive black holes could be found at the centers of this and many
other galaxies), which resolved the concern that quasars were too luminous to be a result of very distant objects or that
a suitable mechanism could not be confirmed to exist in nature. By 1987, it was "well accepted" that this was the
correct explanation for quasars, and the cosmological distance and energy output of quasars were accepted by almost
all researchers.
Modern observations (1970s and onward)
Later, it was found that not all quasars have strong radio emission; in fact, only about 10% are "radio-loud". Hence, the
name "QSO" (quasi-stellar object) is used (in addition to "quasar") to refer to these objects, further categorized into the
"radio-loud" and the "radio-quiet" classes. The discovery of the quasar had large implications for the field of astronomy
in the 1960s, including drawing physics and astronomy closer together.
In 1979, the <color=#3366CC>gravitational lens</color> effect predicted by <color=#3366CC>Albert Einstein</color>'s <color=#3366CC>general theory of relativity</color> was confirmed
observationally for the first time with images of the double quasar 0957+561.
A study published in February 2021 showed that there are more quasars in one direction (towards <color=#3366CC>Hydra</color>) than in the
opposite direction, seemingly indicating that the Earth is moving in that direction. But the direction of this dipole is about
28° away from the direction of the Earth's motion relative to the <color=#3366CC>cosmic microwave background</color> radiation.
In March 2021, a collaboration of scientists, related to the Event Horizon Telescope, presented, for the first time, a

<color=#3366CC>polarized-based image</color> of a <color=#3366CC>black hole</color>, specifically the black hole at the center of <color=#3366CC>Messier 87</color>, an <color=#3366CC>elliptical galaxy</color>
approximately 55 million light-years away in the <color=#3366CC>constellation</color> <color=#3366CC>Virgo</color>, revealing the forces giving rise to quasars.
Current understanding
It is now known that quasars are distant but extremely luminous objects, so any light that reaches the <color=#3366CC>Earth</color> is
redshifted due to the <color=#3366CC>expansion of the universe</color>.
Quasars inhabit the centers of active galaxies and are among the most luminous, powerful, and energetic objects
known in the universe, emitting up to a thousand times the energy output of the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color>, which contains 200–400
billion stars. This radiation is emitted across the electromagnetic spectrum almost uniformly, from X-rays to the far
infrared, with a peak in the ultraviolet optical bands, with some quasars also being strong sources of radio emission and
of gamma-rays. With high-resolution imaging from ground-based telescopes and the <color=#3366CC>Hubble Space Telescope</color>, the
"host galaxies" surrounding the quasars have been detected in some cases. These galaxies are normally too dim to be
seen against the glare of the quasar, except with special techniques. Most quasars, except <color=#3366CC>3C 273</color>, whose average
<color=#3366CC>apparent magnitude</color> is 12.9, cannot be seen with small telescopes.
Quasars are believed—and in many cases confirmed—to be powered by <color=#3366CC>accretion</color> of material into supermassive black
holes in the nuclei of distant galaxies, as suggested in 1964 by <color=#3366CC>Edwin Salpeter</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yakov Zeldovich</color>. Light and other
radiation cannot escape from within the <color=#3366CC>event horizon</color> of a black hole. The energy produced by a quasar is generated
outside the black hole, by gravitational stresses and immense <color=#3366CC>friction</color> within the material nearest to the black hole, as it
orbits and falls inward. The huge luminosity of quasars results from the accretion discs of central supermassive black
holes, which can convert between 5.7% and 32% of the <color=#3366CC>mass</color> of an object into <color=#3366CC>energy</color>, compared to just 0.7% for the
<color=#3366CC>p–p chain</color> <color=#3366CC>nuclear fusion</color> process that dominates the energy production in Sun-like stars. Central masses of 105 to 109
<color=#3366CC>solar masses</color> have been measured in quasars by using reverberation mapping. Several dozen nearby large galaxies,
including the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color> galaxy, that do not have an active center and do not show any activity similar to a quasar, are
confirmed to contain a similar supermassive black hole in their <color=#3366CC>nuclei (galactic center)</color>. Thus, it is now thought that all
large galaxies have a black hole of this kind, but only a small fraction have sufficient matter in the right kind of orbit at
their center to become active and power radiation in such a way as to be seen as quasars.
This also explains why quasars were more common in the early universe, as this energy production ends when the
supermassive black hole consumes all of the gas and dust near it. This means that it is possible that most galaxies,
including the Milky Way, have gone through an active stage, appearing as a quasar or some other class of active
galaxy that depended on the black-hole mass and the accretion rate, and are now quiescent because they lack a
supply of matter to feed into their central black holes to generate radiation.
The matter accreting onto the black hole is unlikely to fall directly in, but will have some angular momentum around the
black hole, which will cause the matter to collect into an <color=#3366CC>accretion disc</color>. Quasars may also be ignited or re-ignited when
normal galaxies merge and the black hole is infused with a fresh source of matter. It has been suggested that a quasar
could form when the <color=#3366CC>Andromeda Galaxy</color> collides with the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color> galaxy in approximately 3–5 billion years.
In the 1980s, unified models were developed in which quasars were classified as a particular kind of <color=#3366CC>active galaxy</color>, and
a consensus emerged that in many cases it is simply the viewing angle that distinguishes them from other active
galaxies, such as <color=#3366CC>blazars</color> and <color=#3366CC>radio galaxies</color>.
The highest-redshift quasar known (As of 2024 8) is UHZ1, with a redshift of approximately 10.1, which corresponds to
a <color=#3366CC>comoving distance</color> of approximately 31.7 billion <color=#3366CC>light-years</color> from Earth (these distances are much larger than the
distance light could travel in the universe's 13.8-billion-year history because the universe is expanding).
Properties
More than 900000 quasars have been found (as of July 2023), most from the <color=#3366CC>Sloan Digital Sky Survey</color>. All observed
quasar spectra have redshifts between 0.056 and 10.1 (as of 2024), which means they range from 600 million to 30
billion <color=#3366CC>light-years away from Earth</color>. Because of the great distances to the farthest quasars and the finite velocity of light,
they and their surrounding space appear as they existed in the very early universe.
The power of quasars originates from supermassive black holes believed to exist at the core of most galaxies. The
Doppler shifts of stars near the cores of galaxies indicate that they are revolving around tremendous masses with very
steep gravity gradients, suggesting black holes.
Although quasars appear faint when viewed from Earth, they are visible from extreme distances, being the most
luminous objects in the known universe. The brightest quasar in the sky is <color=#3366CC>3C 273</color> in the <color=#3366CC>constellation</color> of <color=#3366CC>Virgo</color>. It has an
average <color=#3366CC>apparent magnitude</color> of 12.8 (bright enough to be seen through a medium-sized amateur <color=#3366CC>telescope</color>), but it has
an <color=#3366CC>absolute magnitude</color> of 26.7. From a distance of about 33 light-years, this object would shine in the sky about as
brightly as the <color=#3366CC>Sun</color>. This quasar's <color=#3366CC>luminosity</color> is, therefore, about 4 trillion (4) times that of the Sun, or about 100 times
that of the total light of giant galaxies like the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color>. This assumes that the quasar is radiating energy in all
directions, but the active galactic nucleus is believed to be radiating preferentially in the direction of its jet. In a universe
containing hundreds of billions of galaxies, most of which had active nuclei billions of years ago but only seen today, it
is statistically certain that thousands of energy jets should be pointed toward the Earth, some more directly than others.
In many cases it is likely that the brighter the quasar, the more directly its jet is aimed at the Earth. Such quasars are
called <color=#3366CC>blazars</color>.
The hyper-luminous quasar APM 08279+5255, when discovered in 1998, was given an <color=#3366CC>absolute magnitude</color> of 32.2.
High-resolution imaging with the <color=#3366CC>Hubble Space Telescope</color> and the 10 m <color=#3366CC>Keck Telescope</color> revealed that this system is
<color=#3366CC>gravitationally lensed</color>. A study of the gravitational lensing of this system suggests that the light emitted has been
magnified by a factor of ~10. It is still substantially more luminous than nearby quasars such as 3C 273.
Quasars were much more common in the early universe than they are today. This discovery by Maarten Schmidt in
1967 was early strong evidence against <color=#3366CC>steady-state cosmology</color> and in favor of the <color=#3366CC>Big Bang</color> cosmology. Quasars
show the locations where supermassive black holes are growing rapidly (by <color=#3366CC>accretion</color>). Detailed simulations reported in
2021 showed that galaxy structures, such as spiral arms, use gravitational forces to 'put the brakes on' gas that would
otherwise orbit galaxy centers forever; instead, the braking mechanism enabled the gas to fall into the supermassive
black holes, releasing enormous radiant energies. These black holes co-evolve with the mass of stars in their host
galaxy in a way not fully understood at present. One idea is that jets, radiation, and winds created by the quasars shut
down the formation of new stars in the host galaxy, a process called "feedback". The jets that produce strong radio
emission in some quasars at the centers of <color=#3366CC>clusters of galaxies</color> are known to have enough power to prevent the hot gas
in those clusters from cooling and falling onto the central galaxy.
Quasars' luminosities are variable, with time scales ranging from months to hours. This means that quasars generate
and emit their energy from a very small region, since each part of the quasar would have to be in contact with other
parts on such a time scale as to allow the coordination of the luminosity variations. This would mean that a quasar
varying on a time scale of a few weeks cannot be larger than a few light-weeks across. The emission of large amounts
of power from a small region requires a power source far more efficient than the nuclear fusion that powers stars. The
conversion of gravitational potential energy to radiation by infalling to a black hole converts between 6% and 32% of the
mass to energy, compared to 0.7% for the conversion of mass to energy in a star like the Sun. It is the only process
known that can produce such high power over a very long term. (Stellar explosions such as <color=#3366CC>supernovas</color> and
<color=#3366CC>gamma-ray bursts</color>, and direct <color=#3366CC>matter</color>–<color=#3366CC>antimatter</color> annihilation, can also produce very high power output, but supernovae
only last for days, and the universe does not appear to have had large amounts of antimatter at the relevant times.)
Since quasars exhibit all the properties common to other <color=#3366CC>active galaxies</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>Seyfert galaxies</color>, the emission from
quasars can be readily compared to that of smaller active galaxies powered by smaller supermassive black holes. To
create a luminosity of 1040 <color=#3366CC>watts</color> (the typical brightness of a quasar), a supermassive black hole would have to
consume the material equivalent of 10 solar masses per year. The brightest known quasars devour 1,000 solar masses
of material every year (equivalent to 10 Earths per second). Quasar luminosities can vary considerably over time,
depending on their surroundings. Since it is difficult to fuel quasars for many billions of years, after a quasar finishes
accreting the surrounding gas and dust, it becomes an ordinary galaxy.
Radiation from quasars is partially "nonthermal" (i.e., not due to <color=#3366CC>black-body radiation</color>), and approximately 10% are
observed to also have jets and lobes like those of <color=#3366CC>radio galaxies</color> that also carry significant (but poorly understood)
amounts of energy in the form of particles moving at relativistic speeds. Extremely high energies might be explained by
several mechanisms (see Fermi acceleration and Centrifugal mechanism of acceleration). Quasars can be detected

over the entire observable <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic spectrum</color>, including <color=#3366CC>radio</color>, <color=#3366CC>infrared</color>, <color=#3366CC>visible light</color>, <color=#3366CC>ultraviolet</color>, <color=#3366CC>X-ray</color> and even
<color=#3366CC>gamma rays</color>. Most quasars are brightest in their rest-frame ultraviolet <color=#3366CC>wavelength</color> of 121.6 nm Lyman-alpha emission
line of hydrogen, but due to the tremendous redshifts of these sources, that peak luminosity has been observed as far
to the red as 900.0 nm, in the near infrared. A minority of quasars show strong radio emission, which is generated by
jets of matter moving close to the speed of light. When viewed downward, these appear as <color=#3366CC>blazars</color> and often have
regions that seem to move away from the center faster than the speed of light (<color=#3366CC>superluminal</color> expansion). This is an
optical illusion due to the properties of <color=#3366CC>special relativity</color>.
Quasar redshifts are measured from the strong <color=#3366CC>spectral lines</color> that dominate their visible and ultraviolet emission
spectra. These lines are brighter than the continuous spectrum. They exhibit Doppler broadening corresponding to a
mean speed of several percent of the speed of light. Fast motions strongly indicate a large mass. Emission lines of
hydrogen (mainly of the Lyman series and Balmer series), helium, carbon, magnesium, iron, and oxygen are the
brightest lines. The atoms emitting these lines range from neutral to highly ionized, leaving them highly charged. This
wide range of ionization shows that the gas is highly irradiated by the quasar, not merely hot, and not by stars, which
cannot produce such a wide range of ionization.
Like all (unobscured) active galaxies, quasars can be strong X-ray sources. Radio-loud quasars can also produce
X-rays and gamma rays by <color=#3366CC>inverse Compton scattering</color> of lower-energy photons by the radio-emitting electrons in the
jet.
Iron quasars show strong emission lines resulting from low-ionization <color=#3366CC>iron</color> (Fe II), such as IRAS 18508-7815.
Spectral lines, reionization, and the early universe
Quasars also provide some clues as to the end of the <color=#3366CC>Big Bang</color>'s <color=#3366CC>reionization</color>. The oldest known quasars (<color=#3366CC>z</color> = 6) display
a Gunn–Peterson trough and have absorption regions in front of them, indicating that the <color=#3366CC>intergalactic medium</color> at that
time was neutral gas. More recent quasars show no absorption region, but rather their spectra contain a spiky area
known as the <color=#3366CC>Lyman-alpha forest</color>; this indicates that the intergalactic medium has undergone reionization into <color=#3366CC>plasma</color>,
and that neutral gas exists only in small clouds.
The intense production of <color=#3366CC>ionizing</color> <color=#3366CC>ultraviolet</color> radiation is also significant, as it would provide a mechanism for
reionization to occur as galaxies form. Despite this, current theories suggest that quasars were not the primary source
of reionization; the primary causes of reionization were probably the earliest generations of <color=#3366CC>stars</color>, known as population
III stars (possibly 70%), and <color=#3366CC>dwarf galaxies</color> (very early small high-energy galaxies) (possibly 30%).
Quasars show evidence of elements heavier than <color=#3366CC>helium</color>, indicating that galaxies underwent a massive phase of <color=#3366CC>star</color>
<color=#3366CC>formation</color>, creating population III stars between the time of the <color=#3366CC>Big Bang</color> and the first observed quasars. Light from
these stars may have been observed in 2005 using <color=#3366CC>NASA</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Spitzer Space Telescope</color>, although this observation
remains to be confirmed.
Subtypes
The <color=#3366CC>taxonomy</color> of quasars includes various subtypes representing subsets of the quasar population having distinct
properties.
• Radio-loud quasars are quasars with powerful <color=#3366CC>jets</color> that are strong sources of radio-wavelength emission. These
make up about 10% of the overall quasar population.
• Radio-quiet quasars are those quasars lacking powerful jets, with relatively weaker radio emission than the
radio-loud population. The majority of quasars (about 90%) are radio-quiet.
• Broad absorption-line (BAL) quasars are quasars whose spectra exhibit broad absorption lines that are blue-shifted
relative to the quasar's rest frame, resulting from gas flowing outward from the active nucleus in the direction
toward the observer. Broad absorption lines are found in about 10% of quasars, and BAL quasars are usually
radio-quiet. In the rest-frame ultraviolet spectra of BAL quasars, broad absorption lines can be detected from
ionized carbon, magnesium, silicon, nitrogen, and other elements.
• Type 2 (or Type II) quasars are quasars in which the accretion disc and broad emission lines are highly obscured
by dense gas and <color=#3366CC>dust</color>. They are higher-luminosity counterparts of Type 2 Seyfert galaxies.
• Red quasars are quasars with optical colors that are redder than normal quasars, thought to be the result of
moderate levels of dust <color=#3366CC>extinction</color> within the quasar host galaxy. Infrared surveys have demonstrated that red
quasars make up a substantial fraction of the total quasar population.
• Optically violent variable (OVV) quasars are radio-loud quasars in which the jet is directed toward the observer.
Relativistic beaming of the jet emission results in strong and rapid variability of the quasar brightness. OVV quasars
are also considered to be a type of <color=#3366CC>blazar</color>.
• Weak emission line quasars are quasars having unusually faint emission lines in the ultraviolet/visible spectrum.
Role in celestial reference systems
Because quasars are extremely distant, bright, and small in apparent size, they are useful reference points in
establishing a measurement grid on the sky. The International Celestial Reference System (ICRS) is based on
hundreds of extra-galactic radio sources, mostly quasars, distributed around the entire sky. Because they are so
distant, they are apparently stationary to current technology, yet their positions can be measured with the utmost
accuracy by very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI). The positions of most are known to 0.001 <color=#3366CC>arcsecond</color> or better,
which is orders of magnitude more precise than the best optical measurements.
Multiple quasars
A grouping of two or more quasars on the sky can result from a chance alignment, where the quasars are not physically
associated, from actual physical proximity, or from the effects of gravity bending the light of a single quasar into two or
more images by <color=#3366CC>gravitational lensing</color>. Discerning between these cases can be difficult.
Lensed multiples
A multiple-image quasar is a quasar whose light undergoes <color=#3366CC>gravitational lensing</color>, resulting in double, triple or quadruple
images of the same quasar. The first such gravitational lens to be discovered was the double-imaged quasar
Q0957+561 (or Twin Quasar) in 1979. An example of a triply lensed quasar is PG1115+08. Several quadruple-image
quasars are known, including the Einstein Cross and the Cloverleaf Quasar, with the first such discoveries happening
in the mid-1980s.
The <color=#3366CC>Gaia</color> astrometric all-sky survey has already discovered a dozen or so Einstein crosses, and continued work with its
data releases has the potential to identify many more still.
A relatively recent topic of research called "time delay cosmology" uses multiple-lens quasars to probe the <color=#3366CC>Hubble</color>
<color=#3366CC>tension</color>. When differing images of a single source have differing path lengths, that difference can be measured via the
time delay between flickers in the images. The path length difference, plus modelling the deflecting mass, can be used
to estimate the absolute distance of the source, which enables a cosmic distance measurement independent of the
standard <color=#3366CC>cosmic distance ladder</color>. Some results from 2020, claiming precision of 2-3%, were later determined to suffer
from systematic errors due to overly strong assumptions; in 2025, the TDCOSMO collaboration significantly weakened
the assumptions, publishing a result of 71.6 km/s (around 5% precision).
Physical multiples
When two quasars appear to be very close to each other as seen from Earth (separated by a few <color=#3366CC>arcseconds</color> or less),
they are commonly referred to as a "double quasar". If a visual pair are shown to be also close together in space (i.e.
observed to have similar redshifts), they are termed a "quasar pair", or as a "binary quasar" or "dual quasar" if they are
close enough that their host galaxies are likely to be physically interacting.
As quasars are overall rare objects in the universe, the probability of three or more separate quasars being found near
the same physical location is very low, and determining whether the system is closely separated physically requires
significant observational effort, which most quasar-like sources never receive; as a result, not many physical multiple
quasars are known.
Physical multiple quasars can be important mechanisms to study <color=#3366CC>galactic interactions</color> and evolution, especially in the
early universe, such as when star formation and galactic activity were highest (redshift z=2).
The <color=#3366CC>Gaia</color> astrometric all-sky survey, in its first foray into multiple quasars, suggested that the <color=#3366CC>Sloan Digital Sky</color>
<color=#3366CC>Survey</color>–discovered quasar J0749+2255 was in fact a dual quasar. Follow-up observations by Hubble, Keck, Gemini,
Chandra, and VLA confirmed the true nature of this source, an interacting galaxy pair at redshift z=2.17. Future work
with Gaia data releases can be expected to significantly expand the catalog of both lensed and physical multiple
quasars, and associated galactic research.
The first true triple quasar was found in 2007 by observations at the <color=#3366CC>W. M. Keck Observatory</color> in <color=#3366CC>Mauna Kea</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color>.
LBQS 1429-008 (or QQQ J1432-0106) was first observed in 1989 and at the time was found to be a double quasar.
When <color=#3366CC>astronomers</color> discovered the third member, they confirmed that the sources were separate and not the result of
gravitational lensing. This triple quasar has a redshift of z = 2.076. The components are separated by an estimated
30–50 <color=#3366CC>kiloparsecs</color> (roughly 97,000–160,000 light-years), which is typical for interacting galaxies. In 2013, the second
true triplet of quasars, QQQ J1519+0627, was found with a redshift z = 1.51, the whole system fitting within a physical
separation of 25 kpc (about 80,000 light-years).
The first true quadruple quasar system was discovered in 2015 at a redshift z = 2.0412 and has an overall physical
scale of about 200 kpc (roughly 650,000 light-years).
